title: AI-Assisted Scholarly Writing in Education: A Scoping Review (2019–2024)
venue: Вестник КазНПУ имени Абая, серия «Педагогические науки»
extended_summary:
This paper asks what research has been published from 2019 to 2024 on AI-assisted scholarly writing in educational settings, and what research methods, concepts, and findings characterize this emerging literature. The authors frame the topic around rapid growth in generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and automated writing evaluation systems, and they use a scoping review approach following PRISMA-ScR to map the field rather than test a single intervention themselves.

The review synthesizes empirical and conceptual studies identified through major academic databases. It describes the main uses of AI in writing education, including drafting support, writing feedback, automated evaluation, plagiarism detection, and human–AI collaboration. The paper notes that the literature includes qualitative studies, surveys, quasi-experiments, mixed-methods case studies, and a small number of systematic reviews, with most work concentrated in higher education but some evidence from high school contexts as well.

The main conclusion is that AI-assisted writing tools are generally reported to improve writing efficiency, engagement, and sometimes writing performance, but they also raise concerns about plagiarism, over-reliance, and the need for AI literacy. The authors emphasize that the field is still methodologically immature: there are few longitudinal studies, few large controlled experiments, inconsistent definitions of AI assistance, and limited theoretical grounding. They recommend clearer reporting, stronger designs, and better integration of learning theory in future work.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed scoping review, which is methodologically transparent but not a causal study and does not provide pooled quantitative estimates. The evidence base summarized is mostly qualitative, survey, and small quasi-experimental work, so credibility for intervention effects is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful benefits for writing efficiency and student perceptions, but it does not establish causal effect sizes or generalizable impact for K-12 science inquiry support. Its strongest contribution is framing and identifying gaps rather than demonstrating measured impact.

interventions.use_case: Scoping review of AI-assisted scholarly writing tools in education, including generative AI writing assistants such as ChatGPT and automated writing evaluation tools such as Grammarly/ETS e-rater for drafting, editing, and feedback on student writing.
Automated writing evaluation and feedback systems that score or comment on student writing, including tools like Writerly, Google Docs feedback, Grammarly, and ETS e-rater.
Generative AI chatbots and large-language-model writing assistants, especially ChatGPT, used to help generate ideas, draft text, and support academic writing tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This scoping review synthesizes studies of AI-assisted writing in education and concludes that most recent work reports improved writing efficiency, drafting support, and sometimes higher writing performance. However, the review also notes risks such as superficial writing, plagiarism concerns, and inconsistent evidence, especially because few studies are longitudinal or large-scale. No pooled effect size is reported because this is a scoping review, not a meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Writing performance, writing efficiency, student perceptions, and reported writing quality across included studies

finding.finding_summary: Across the included literature, students generally reported positive perceptions of AI writing tools, describing them as helpful, engaging, and motivating during writing tasks. The review also notes that students appreciated AI support for idea generation and drafting, although concerns about integrity sometimes tempered these views. No effect size is reported in the review.
finding.measure: Student attitudes, perceptions, motivation, and engagement reported in surveys, interviews, and case studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies AI literacy and responsible use as recurring needs, suggesting that effective AI-assisted writing depends on prompt skills, judgment, and critical evaluation of AI outputs. At the same time, it warns that over-reliance on AI may reduce depth of thinking and produce superficial writing, but these concerns are not yet backed by many rigorous causal studies.
finding.measure: AI literacy, responsible-use awareness, and concerns about critical thinking/superficial writing

finding.finding_summary: The reviewed studies commonly report that AI tools improve writing efficiency, speed of drafting, and ease of editing or revision. This is a recurring qualitative and survey-based finding across the literature, but the scoping review does not synthesize a numerical estimate of time savings.
finding.measure: Writing efficiency, drafting speed, and perceived productivity

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is the need for clearer policy, academic integrity guidance, and AI literacy training in institutions. The review argues that current evidence is fragmented and that schools and universities need standards for acceptable AI use, transparency, and assessment design, but it does not test policy interventions directly.
finding.measure: Policy and governance implications, academic integrity concerns, and recommendations for institutional guidance
